(3) Each of the Promoter Selling Shareholders have, severally and not jointly, authorized its participation in the Offer for Sale to the extent of its respective

and 366, respectively.
(4) The Employee Reservation portion shall not exceed 5% of our post-Offer equity share capital. In the event of an under-subscription in the Employee 
Reservation Portion, the unsubscribed portion may be Allotted on a proportionate basis to Eligible Employees Bidding in the Employee Reservation 
Portion, for a value in excess of ₹ 200,000 (net of Employee Discount, if any), subject to the total Allotment to an Eligible Employee not exceeding ₹ 
500,000 (net of Employee Discount, if any) The unsubscribed portion if any, in the Employee Reservation Portion (after allocation up to ₹ 500,000 (net 
of Employee Discount, if any), shall be added back to the Net Offer. Further, an Eligible Employee Bidding in the Employee Reservation Portion can 
also Bid in the Net Offer and such Bids will not be treated as multiple Bids subject to applicable limits. Our Company, in consultation with the BRLMs,

6. Compliance with the Companies Act, 1956 and the Companies Act, 2013
All issuances of equity shares since the date of incorporation of our Company, have been in compliance with the relevant 
provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 and Companies Act, 2013. Further, the Company has not issued any other securities 
since its incorporation. However, our Company has filed a compounding application dated September 4, 2025 in relation 
to certain equity shares bought back in July 2021 and pursuant to a final order dated February 12, 2026, a fine of ₹0.75 
million was levied (₹0.38 million on our Company and ₹0.38 million on the officer in default), which has been paid, and 
the requisite filings have been made with the RoC. For details of the complete set of corporate resolutions, filings, and 
other records, in relation to changes in our issued, subscribed and paid-up share capital that are untraceable in our records, 
please see “Risk Factors- We have filed compounding and adjudication applications with the competent regulatory 
authorities in relation to past non-compliances under the Companies Act, which are pending as of the date of this Red 
Herring Prospectus. There can be no assurance that these applications will have a favourable outcome or that penalties 
will not be imposed, which may impact our financial condition and reputation”.

d) Details of share capital locked-in for six months or any other period as may be prescribed under applicable law
In terms of Regulation 17 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, except for the Minimum Promoters’ Contribution and any 
Equity Shares held by our Promoters in excess of Minimum Promoter’s Contribution, which shall be locked in as 
above, the entire pre-Offer Equity Share capital of our Company, shall, unless otherwise permitted under the SEBI 
ICDR Regulations, be locked in for a period of six months from the date of Allotment in the Offer. In terms of 
Regulation 17(c) of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, Equity Shares held by a venture capital fund or alternative investment 
fund of category I or category II or a foreign venture capital investor shall not be locked-in for a period of six months 
from the date of Allotment, provided that such Equity Shares shall be locked in for a period of at least six months from 
the date of purchase by such shareholders.
In terms of Regulation 22 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, Equity Shares held by our Promoters which are locked-in 
pursuant to Regulation 16 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, may be transferred amongst our Promoters or any member 
of the Promoter Group or to any new promoter, subject to continuation of lock-in in the hands of the transferees for 
the remaining period and compliance with provisions of the SEBI Takeover Regulations, as applicable and such 
transferee shall not be eligible to transfer them till the lock-in period stipulated in SEBI ICDR Regulations has expired. 
The Equity Shares held by persons other than our Promoters and locked-in pursuant to Regulation 17 of the SEBI 
ICDR Regulations, may be transferred to any other person holding Equity Shares which are locked-in, subject to the

26. Employee Stock Option Plan
HD Fire Protect Limited – Employee Stock Option Plan 2025 (“ESOP Plan”)
Pursuant to a resolution of our Board of Directors dated September 9, 2025, and Shareholders’ resolution dated September 
10, 2025, our Company had instituted an employee stock option plan, the ESOP Plan. As on the date of this Red Herring 
Prospectus, a total of 650,442 options have been granted pursuant to resolutions of the NRC Committee dated July 20, 
2026, and September 12, 2026.
Pursuant to the ESOP Plan, options to acquire Equity Shares may be granted to eligible “employees” including (i) 
permanent employee of the Company, who is working in India or outside India; or (ii) a director of the Company, whether 
a whole time director or not, excluding an independent director of the Company; or (iii) an employee as defined in (i) or 
(ii) above, of a subsidiary, in India or outside India, or a holding company but excludes an employee who is a promoter or 
a person belonging to the promoter group; or a director who either himself or through his relatives or through anybody 
corporate, directly or indirectly, holds more than ten percent of the outstanding equity shares of the Company.
Under the ESOP Scheme, the Board and/or the NRC Committee is authorised to issue Equity Shares of the Company 
pursuant to exercise of options granted under the ESOP Scheme not exceeding 1,350,000 Equity Shares of face value of ₹ 
5 each to the eligible employees in one or more tranches, from time to time. During any one year, no employee shall be 
granted options exceeding 200,000 options at the time of grant of options.

by M/s RDA & Associates, Independent Chartered Accountant, pursuant to their certificate dated October 5, 2026.

OBJECTS OF THE OFFER
The objects of the Offer are to (i) to carry out the Offer for Sale of up to 26,284,500 Equity Shares of face value of ₹5 each by 
the Promoter Selling Shareholders aggregating up to ₹ [●] million; and (ii) achieve the benefits of listing the Equity Shares on 
the Stock Exchanges. For further details of the Offer, see “The Offer” on page 76.
Further, our Company expects that listing of the Equity Shares will enhance our visibility and brand image and provide liquidity 
and a public market for the Equity Shares in India.
Utilization of the Offer Proceeds by the Promoter Selling Shareholders
Our Company will not receive any proceeds from the Offer (the “Offer Proceeds”) and all the Offer Proceeds will be received 
by the Promoter Selling Shareholders after deduction of Offer related expenses and relevant taxes thereon, to be borne by the
Promoter Selling Shareholders. For details of the Offered Shares, see “Other Regulatory and Statutory Disclosure—Authority 
for the Offer” on page 366.
Offer expenses
The Offer expenses are estimated to be approximately ₹ [●] million.
The Offer expenses comprises of, among other things, listing fee, underwriting fees, selling commission and brokerage, fees 
payable to the Book Running Lead Managers, legal counsel, Registrar to the Offer, Escrow Collection Bank, processing fee to 
the SCSBs for processing ASBA Forms submitted by ASBA Bidders procured by the Syndicate and submitted to SCSBs, 
brokerage and selling commission payable to Registered Brokers, RTAs and CDPs, fees payable to the Sponsor Bank(s) for 
Bids made by UPI Bidders, printing and stationery expenses, advertising and marketing expenses and all other incidental 
expenses for listing the Equity Shares on the Stock Exchanges.
Other than (a) the listing fees, audit fees of the Statutory Auditors (other than to the extent attributable to the Offer) and expenses 
in relation to product or corporate advertisements of our Company in consistent with our past practices (other than expenses in 
relation to the marketing and advertising undertaken specifically for the Offer) each of which will be borne solely by our 
Company; and (b) fees and expenses in relation to the legal counsel to the Promoter Selling Shareholders which shall be borne 
by the Promoter Selling Shareholders, all Offer Expenses including, among other things, filing fees, book building fees and 
other charges, fees and expenses of the SEBI, the Stock Exchanges, the Registrar of Companies and any other governmental 
authority, advertising, printing, road show expenses, accommodation and travel expenses, fees and expenses of the Indian legal 
counsel to our Company and the Indian to the BRLMs, fees and expenses of the Statutory Auditors for the Offer and, registrar 
fees and broker fees (including fees for procuring of applications), bank charges, fees and, expenses of the BRLMs, syndicate
members, Self Certified Syndicate Banks, other Designated Intermediaries and any other consultant, advisor or third party in 
connection with the Offer shall be borne by the Promoter Selling Shareholders in proportion to the number of Equity Shares 
transferred by each Promoter Selling Shareholder in the Offer, except as may be prescribed by the SEBI or any other regulatory 
authority. All such payments shall be made by our Company in the first instance on behalf of the Promoter Selling Shareholders 
and the Promoter Selling Shareholders agree that it shall, severally and not jointly, reimburse our Company out of the Offer 
proceeds in proportion to their respective Offered Shares, for any expenses incurred by our Company on behalf of such Promoter
Selling Shareholders. In the event that the Offer is postponed or withdrawn or abandoned for any reason or the Offer is not 
successful or consummated, all costs and expenses with respect to the Offer which may have accrued up to the date of such 
postponement, withdrawal, abandonment or failure shall be borne by the Promoter Selling Shareholders in proportion to the 
number of Equity Shares the Promoter Selling Shareholders has agreed to sell in the Offer as will be disclosed in this Red 
Herring Prospectus to be filed by the Company with the SEBI in relation to the Offer. The Promoter Selling Shareholders agrees 
that it shall reimburse our Company for any expenses in relation to the Offer paid by our Company on behalf of the Promoter 
Selling Shareholders directly from the Public Offer Account in the manner as may be set out in the relevant agreements.
All the expenses relating to the Offer shall be paid by our Company in the first instance. Upon commencement of listing and 
trading of the Equity Shares on the Stock Exchanges pursuant to the Offer, each Promoter Selling Shareholder shall reimburse 
our Company for any expenses in relation to the Offer paid by our Company on behalf of each of the Promoter Selling 
Shareholders directly from the Public Offer Account, in proportion to the Equity Shares offered in the Offer by each Promoter
Selling Shareholder.
In the event the Offer is postponed, withdrawn or not consummated, for any reason whatsoever, or the Offer is not successful 
or consummated, the Promoter Selling Shareholders shall reimburse to our Company the Offer expenses that have accrued until 
such date in proportion to the Equity Shares offered in the Offer by each Promoter Selling Shareholder.

The Price Band and Offer Price will be determined by our Company, in consultation with the BRLMs, on the basis of assessment 
of market demand for the Equity Shares offered through the Book Building Process and on the basis of the quantitative and 
qualitative factors described below. The face value of the Equity Shares is ₹ 5 each and the Offer Price is [●] times the face 
value at the lower end of the Price Band and [●] times the face value at the higher end of the Price Band.

“Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations” beginning on pages 21, 210, 282
and 327 respectively, to have an informed view before making an investment decision.

Some of the qualitative factors and our strengths which form the basis for computing the Offer Price are: 
1. Well established global presence in a certification and stringent empanelment driven, high barrier industry.
2. Comprehensive equipment and systems portfolio with presence across diverse end use sectors.
3. Strong and diversified customer base with long standing global customer relationships.
4. Advanced design and manufacturing capabilities, well equipped to deliver high quality fire protection equipment and 
systems with consistent R&D and innovation.
5. Experienced management team and qualified personnel with significant industry experience.
6. Track record of profitability and consistent financial performance.
For further details, see “Our Business – Competitive Strengths” on page 213.

(1) Revenue from Operations is as per Restated Financial Information refers to income earned by an entity from its core business activities including Sale of 
goods, Rendering services and Other operating revenue 
(2) Domestic Revenue represents revenue stream specific to India.
(3) Export Revenue represents revenue stream specific to outside India. 
(4) Operating EBITDA is calculated as restated profit before tax plus finance costs, depreciation and amortization expense less other income.
(5) Operating EBITDA margin is calculated as Operating EBITDA divided by Revenue from Operations
(6) Profit After Tax (PAT) for the year is as per Restated Financial Information 
(7) PAT Margin is calculated as profit after tax (PAT) as a percentage of Total Income.
(8) Return on equity (RoE) is calculated as PAT divided by Average Tangible Net worth. Tangible Net worth is calculated as Total Equity subtracted by 
Intangible Assets
(9) Return on capital employed (RoCE) is calculated as earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) divided by the Average capital employed. EBIT is calculated 
as the restated profit after tax for the year/ period plus total tax expense plus finance costs and capital employed is calculated as the sum of Tangible Net 
worth and total borrowings
(10) Fixed Asset Turnover Ratio is calculated as Revenue from Operations divided by Average Property, plant and equipment, Capital work-in-progress and 
Right-to-use assets.
(11) Inventory days is calculated as average inventory divided by Cost of Sales, multiplied by 365. However, for the three months ended June 30, 2026, inventory 
days is calculated as inventories divided by Cost of Sales for the given period multiplied by 90 days. Cost of Sales is calculated as total expenses less 
Finance cost and Depreciation and amortization
(12) Trade Receivable days is calculated as average trade receivable divided by Revenue from Operations, multiplied by 365. However, for the three months 
ended June 30, 2026, trade receivable days is calculated as trade receivables divided by Revenue from Operations for the given period multiplied by 90 
days.
(13) Trade payable days is calculated as average trade payable divided by Cost of Goods Sold (COGS), multiplied by 365. However, for the three months 
ended June 30, 2026, trade payable days is calculated as trade payables divided by Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) for the given period multiplied by 90 days. 
COGS is calculated as the sum of Cost of materials consumed, Purchase of stock-in-trade and change in inventories of finished goods, stock-in-trade and 
work-in-progress.
(14) Cash conversion cycle is calculated as the sum of trade receivable days and inventory days, less trade payable days.

Global macroeconomic overview
Global GDP to grow by 3.0% in CY26 and 3.4% in CY27
According to the World Economic Outlook: July 2026 Update published by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the global 
economic environment is currently being influenced by two contrasting developments with varying implications across 
countries. On one hand, the ongoing conflict in the Middle East has created a negative supply-side shock, affecting commodity 
markets and trade flows. On the other hand, rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and its increasing adoption across 
industries have strengthened the global technology cycle, providing a positive impetus to economic activity. While the 
magnitude of these effects differs across economies, the IMF projects global GDP growth at 3.0% in 2026, rising to 3.4% in 
2027. The improvement reflects the expected support from technology-driven investment and demand, which is anticipated to 
partly offset the adverse economic consequences of the Middle East conflict. Global headline inflation is forecast to increase 
from 4.1% in 2025 to 4.7% in 2026, largely due to higher energy and food prices, before moderating to 3.9% in 2027.
The IMF's projections are based on the following assumptions:
• Maritime trade through the Strait of Hormuz is expected to resume gradually from mid-July, with conditions 
normalising and returning broadly to pre-conflict levels by March 2027.
• Existing trade policy measures, including those initially introduced as temporary arrangements, are assumed to remain 
in place throughout the forecast period.
• Geopolitical tensions and policy-related uncertainty are expected to stay elevated through 2027.
• The momentum of the AI-led technology cycle is assumed to moderate over time, with no additional external boost to 
productivity growth.

India benefits from a large and young workforce with highly competitive wage levels compared with developed economies and

Ease of doing business
India has undertaken significant reforms to improve its investment climate, resulting in a marked improvement in the World 
Bank’s Ease of Doing Business rankings over the past decade. Key reforms include the digitalisation of compliance processes, 
simplification of procedures for starting businesses, fast-tracking of environmental clearances and implementation of the goods 
and services tax (GST). These reforms have had a positive impact on investor sentiment and facilitated an increase in foreign
direct investment (FDI) in manufacturing-led sectors such as electronics, defence, renewable energy and automobiles.
Nonetheless, state-level disparities persist, particularly in areas such as contract enforcement, land acquisition and utility 
reliability. While Maharashtra, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu have established strong industrial ecosystems, others require more 
policy and infrastructure development to attract meaningful investment.
153
As per the Doing Business Report 2020 by World Bank, India’s rank improved from 142 in 2014 to 63 in 2019, marking an 
advancement of 79 positions over five years.
Global supply chain diversification
In recent years, global manufacturing companies have been actively pursuing diversification to reduce dependence on single￾country sourcing models, particularly due to the pandemic-induced disruptions and rising geopolitical uncertainties. The supply 
chain derisking strategy has resulted in increased interest in India as a manufacturing destination.
India has emerged as a preferred alternative, driven by government initiatives such as the PLI schemes. Aligned with the vision 
of Atmanirbhar Bharat and the Make in India initiative, the PLI scheme aims to strengthen manufacturing, reduce reliance on 
imports and balance growth with sustainability.
As part of Make in India initiative, the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes have been implemented across 14 
key sectors, namely Large-Scale Electronics Manufacturing (LSEM), IT Hardware, Pharmaceuticals, Bulk Drugs, Medical 
Devices, Automobiles and Auto Components, Advanced Chemistry Cell Batteries, Solar PV modules, Telecom & Networking 
Products, Food Processing. The PLI schemes have generated investments exceeding Rs. 2.2 trillion as of 31st December 2025. 
The investments made under the PLI Schemes have led to incremental production and sales of over Rs. 20.4 trillion, as of 
31st December 2025. Further, the Schemes have resulted in an employment generation of over 1.4 million (direct and indirect), 
and 836 applications have been approved across all 14 sectors covered under the PLI framework.
India’s effort to develop domestic manufacturing is bolstered by the global supply chain derisking adopted by global peers This 
strategy involves companies diversifying their operations to limit exposure to single geographic location. The approach is being
considered by some businesses to reduce their dependence on certain countries and diversify their supply chains amidst evolving 
regulatory environment and geopolitical uncertainties. Countries like India, Vietnam, Malaysia and Thailand present potential

Evolution of fire protection regulations in India
Source: Crisil Intelligence
The history of fire services in India spans over two centuries. After Independence, in view of the shortcomings in fire services 
in different states, the government formed a Standing Fire Advisory Committee in 1956 under the Ministry of Home Affairs. 
The committee had the mandate to examine technical problems relating to fire services and advise the government on the 
measures needed for speedy development and upgrades. Fire services fall under the 12th schedule of the Constitution, which 
deals with functions of a municipality.
As urban environments evolved and the emphasis on public safety increased, fire safety and prevention measures were 
integrated into key regulatory instruments, including the National Building Code (NBC) and the Model Building Byelaws 
(MBBL).
The NBC, 2016 – Part 4: Fire and Life Safety forms the central technical reference for fire safety regulations in the country. 
It is the basis upon which state-level legislation, municipal approvals and industrial fire safety protocols are structured. NBC 
2016 is adopted either directly or through incorporation into state-specific fire protection legislation and development control 
regulations. Fire safety regulations have continued to evolve, as multiple states introduce/ amend laws, guidelines and rules, 
such as the Maharashtra Fire Prevention and Life Safety Measures (Amendment) Act, 2023, the Gujarat Fire Prevention and 
Life Safety Measures Regulations, 2023, and the Tamil Nadu Fire and Rescue Services Act, 2025.

Qualitative overview of key fire suppression products
Fire suppression systems are designed to control and extinguish fires automatically or manually, typically using agents such as 
water, gas or foam. Major types of fire suppression systems are as follows:
• Water-based fire suppression systems: These are the most common type of fire suppression equipment. They use 
water to extinguish fires by cooling the fuel. These systems are generally effective in suppressing Class A fires, which 
involve ordinary combustible materials such as wood, paper and cloth. Water-based systems are typically used in 
residential spaces, commercial buildings and industrial settings, and are often connected to a municipal water supply 
or a stored water tank
159
• Gas-based fire suppression systems (using gases and chemicals): These systems use a clean agent gas to extinguish 
fires, although the extinguishing mechanism varies depending on the type of agent used. Inert gas systems function 
primarily by reducing the oxygen concentration in the affected area to a level insufficient to sustain combustion. Clean 
agent systems, function primarily by absorbing heat from the fire and chemically interfering with the combustion 
reaction. It should be noted that not all gaseous systems rely on both mechanisms simultaneously; the specific mode 
of action depends on the agent employed. These systems are typically effective for Class A, B and C fires. Gas-based 
systems are generally used in commercial and industrial settings, such as data centres, laboratories and manufacturing 
facilities. They are designed to extinguish fires quickly without damaging sensitive equipment or leaving residue. They 
are also environmentally friendly and non-corrosive, making them a preferred choice for protecting high-value assets 
and sensitive equipment.
Chemical-based fire suppression systems use a chemical agent, such as dry chemical powder, to extinguish fires by 
interrupting the chemical reaction that sustains combustion. These systems are typically effective for all classes of 
fires, depending on the type of chemical used. Chemical-based systems are generally used in residential, commercial 
and industrial settings, such as kitchens, laboratories and manufacturing facilities. They are designed to extinguish 
fires quickly; however, unlike gas-based systems, dry chemical powder does leave residue upon discharge. This 
residue can be corrosive or abrasive in nature and may cause damage to sensitive electronics or equipment. 
Consequently, these systems are generally considered less suitable than gas-based systems for the protection of high￾value electronic assets, and post-discharge cleanup is typically required.
• Foam equipment & suppression systems: These systems use a foam agent to extinguish fires by smothering the fuel 
and cooling the surrounding area. These systems are typically effective for Class A and Class B fires, which involve 
flammable liquids such as gasoline, oil and paint. Foam equipment & suppression systems are generally used in high￾risk areas such as industries and factories. They are designed to quickly extinguish fires and prevent re-ignition and 
are often used in conjunction with other fire suppression systems.

Exports and imports of key fire protection equipment
Based on an analysis of key export segments in the fire protection equipment, the exports of Indian fire protection equipment
clocked a CAGR of 8% over fiscals 2020-2026 to reach $107 million in fiscal 2026 as compared to $67 million in fiscal 2020. 
This can be attributed to the government's growing focus on the manufacturing sector, coupled with players increasingly 
prioritising branded products and global approvals, which have collectively supported manufacturers. Fire extinguishers, fire
alarms, and fire protection valves are among the key products exported from India, with exports accounting for 8 to 10% of the 
overall fire protection industry in the country.
On the imports front, in the early 1990s, critical fire protection equipment and systems such as deluge valves, alarm valves, and 
medium velocity water spray nozzles were largely imported, owing to the limited availability of Indian manufacturers offering
high-quality alternatives such as UL Listed and FM Approved products. In line with the growth in exports, imports increased 
to $210 million in fiscal 2026 from $104 million in fiscal 2020, reflecting a CAGR of 12%.
In terms of product categories, fire suppression equipment constitutes the majority of trade in the Indian fire protection market. 
The fire detection segment comprises products such as fire alarms, while the fire suppression segment includes fire 
extinguishers, safety valves, and similar products. The fire suppression segment accounted for 91% of exports in the last fiscal, 
valued at ~$97 million, with the balance attributable to the fire detection segment, valued at ~$9 million. Similarly, on the
imports side, fire suppression products comprised 90% of imports in the last fiscal, valued at ~$188 million, while fire detection 
products accounted for the remaining 10%, valued at ~$22 million.
In terms of geographies, the UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA), Singapore, Malaysia, and Vietnam are 
the key export destinations for fire protection products from India. On the other hand, China, the US, Germany, Vietnam, and 
South Korea are the key countries from which fire protection equipment is imported into the country.

Improving consumer awareness
Growing consumer awareness about fire hazards due to educational initiatives, media coverage and more stringent regulations 
has led to an emphasis on fire safety protocols by institutional as well as retail buyers. For example, Union Ministry of Health 
and Family Welfare, in partnership with all States and Union Territories and in coordination with relevant Central Ministries 
and Departments, commenced the nationwide observance of Fire Safety Week from 4th May to 10th May 2026, for prioritising 
and highlighting the issue of fire prevention and safety. This growing awareness is expected to positively influence the demand 
for fire protection equipment by encouraging compliance with the existing fire safety codes and supporting voluntary adoption.
Rising demand for smart fire protection systems and technological advancements
The integration of Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI) and sensory-driven automation has revolutionised the 
fire protection infrastructure, enabling the development of modern and sophisticated systems. For instance, AI-powered systems 
can analyse data from various sources to identify potential fire hazards and enable real-time monitoring, while IoT-enabled 
devices provide real-time monitoring of fire protection systems, enabling a quick response to potential fires and reducing the 
risk of false alarms.
As a result, critical sectors such as oil and gas, data centres, pharmaceuticals and high-value assets, including commercial spaces 
and REITs with a focus on ESG, are expected to be early adopters of these advanced fire protection systems. The adoption of 
these systems will enhance the overall effectiveness and operational reliability of fire protection infrastructure, driving demand 
across industries, particularly in areas where automation, data analytics and centralised controls are prioritised, and supporting 
the growth of smart fire protection systems in high-hazard industries and critical infrastructure.

Government initiatives aimed at strengthening fire protection infrastructure and creating awareness are expected to bring a 
positive influence on the demand of fire suppression equipment in India.

example, Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, in partnership with all States and Union Territories and in 
coordination with relevant Central Ministries and Departments, commenced the nationwide observance of Fire Safety 
Week from 4th May to 10th May 2026, for prioritising and highlighting the issue of fire prevention and safety.
• These awareness campaigns are expected to increase consumer awareness and adoption of fire safety measures, which 
in turn is expected to drive the demand for fire protection equipment
Regulatory requirements-driven growth drivers
Strict regulatory framework and implementation
The government’s increasing focus on fire safety has led to the introduction of stricter building codes, insurance requirements 
and regular fire safety campaigns. These initiatives have increased awareness about the importance of fire safety and driven the
adoption of fire protection equipment in residential, commercial and industrial spaces, directly contributing to the demand for 
fire protection equipment in India. Further, improving the compliance environment regarding fire safety, including increasing
fire safety campaigns by the governments, is also expected to boost the demand for fire protection equipment.
Positive policy and robust FDI support
India's FDI inflows improved to $94.5 billion in fiscal 2026, compared with $36.0 billion in fiscal 2014, reflecting enhanced
investor confidence. This growth has been supported by reforms such as the liberalisation of FDI norms across key sectors, the 
introduction of the GST, and initiatives such as the Make in India programme. To sustain this trajectory, the government 
continues to undertake measures aimed at attracting greater FDI, including the removal of regulatory barriers, streamlining of 
processes, development of infrastructure, strengthening of logistics, and improvement of the overall business environment 
through enhancements to the Ease of Doing Business (EoDB). Notably, through the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) 
Act, 2023, the government has decriminalised 183 provisions across 42 central acts spanning 19 ministries and departments, 
with a view to enhancing the ease of living and the EoDB.
Policy reforms such as these, aimed at improving the ease of doing business and permitting greater FDI in core sectors, including 
manufacturing, are expected to have a positive bearing on the establishment of new industrial facilities in India by both domestic 
and international players.
Collectively, these reforms are expected to attract higher FDI inflows into India, including in fire-intensive sub-sectors such as 
pharmaceuticals and non-conventional energy. This, in turn, is expected to positively influence the development of the 
manufacturing sector, which remains a key end-use segment for fire protection equipment. As these manufacturing units are 
required to adhere to fire safety norms to minimise the risk of loss of life and property, they are, in turn, expected to drive

Certification process
Major certification processes involve a comprehensive and rigorous evaluation of products, systems or services to ensure 
compliance with specific standards and requirements. The certification process consists of three major steps:
• The initial phase: This phase includes the application process, documentation and technical clarification. The 
applicant submits their application, provides necessary documentation and clarifies technical aspects of their product 
or system in the initial phase, setting the foundation for subsequent steps and ensuring that necessary information is 
gathered and reviewed.
• The evaluation and testing phase: This phase involves a thorough assessment of the product or system, including 
site visits, product checking, quality checking, document verification, system checks and other evaluations to verify 
181
compliance with the relevant standards. This phase is critical in ensuring that the product or system meets the required 
specifications and performance criteria.
• The certification and monitoring phase: The certification and monitoring phase is the final phase, which involves 
finalising technical matters, verifying compliance, completing documentation and issuing the certificate. This phase 
also includes regular audits and monitoring to ensure ongoing compliance and maintenance of the certified product or 
system, providing assurance to stakeholders that the certified entity continues to meet the required standards.

To obtain these certifications, companies must undergo multiple testing and inspection processes. Additionally, although these 
processes generally do not have any expiry date, regular audits are required for valid certifications. For example, for 
certifications by UL Solutions and FM Approvals, product-level approval is obtained after a stringent testing procedure, and 
quarterly audits may be required for products post-approval. The entire approval process can be lengthy (1-2 years) as well as 
expensive (cost can run up to Rs 10 million and above).
• Additionally, some companies, especially in the B2B segment, maintain vendor lists, which include manufacturers/ 
companies that are eligible to provide fire protection equipment to the company. The entire process of becoming an 
approved vendor is usually time-consuming and complex, requiring significant time and resources to meet the required 
standards and certifications.
Overall, the certification process for fire suppression equipment and systems can be complex and time-consuming, requiring 
companies to conform to multiple standards, certifications and laws depending on the project requirements. Furthermore,

Assessment of the fire suppression equipment market
Fire suppression systems, also known as firefighting or fire response systems, are an integral component of modern fire 
protection infrastructure, designed to detect and extinguish fires at an early stage, thereby minimising harm to life and property.
The primary objective of a fire suppression system is to respond rapidly to fire outbreaks, often before human intervention is 
possible, usually using a suitable extinguishing agent that is compatible with the nature of fire, as well as characteristics of the 
protected environment. For the same reasons, the selection of a suitable fire suppression system is guided by multiple factors, 
including the type of occupancy, classification of fire hazard, equipment vulnerability and operational continuity requirements. 
Key fire suppression equipment includes fire sprinklers, fire hydrants, hydrant valves, deluge valves and pre-action systems, 
monitors & monitor nozzles, fire nozzles, hose reels, hose boxes, foam equipment & suppression systems, gas-based products, 
and fire blankets.
Overall, these systems function as active fire suppression mechanisms and are typically installed in an environment where fire 
risk is high, and the value of protected assets is significant. Furthermore, deployment of these systems is often mandated by
building codes, fire safety regulations and industry-specific management standards.
For details on major types of suppression systems, please refer to the ‘Qualitative overview of key fire suppression products’ 
section.

Foam equipment & suppression systems
The manufacturing process of foam equipment & suppression systems requires careful control of raw materials, mixing, and 
foaming processes to ensure that the final product meets the required fire protection standards and regulations. Fire-fighting 
foam is mixture of hydrocarbon surfactants, fluoro surfactants, solvents, foam stabilisers, polymers, glycols, etc. The foam is 
typically discharged through a dispensing gun or nozzle, which allows for precise control over the amount and direction of the 
foam. After discharge, the foam expands to fill the gap and provides a fire-resistant seal. The foam is usually stored in 
pressurised containers or tanks, which are designed to maintain the foam's stability and prevent degradation. It is recommended 
to store the foam in a cool, dry place, away from direct sunlight and heat sources, with an ideal storage temperature typically 
ranging from 15°C to 49°C (-22°F to 120°F), but specific recommendations can vary. Storage temperature ranges are crucial 
for maintaining the foam concentrate's effectiveness and preventing damage to the container.

Overview of the global fire suppression equipment market
Global fire suppression equipment market is expected to clock a CAGR of ~6.5-7.5% between CY2025-2030
The global demand for fire suppression systems is being driven by the rising awareness of fire safety norms and the losses 
caused by fire incidents, particularly in high-value assets and critical infrastructure. The expansion of commercial real estate, 
including shopping malls, hotels, hospitals, airports and large public spaces, is also fuelling demand, as these facilities require 
sophisticated suppression solutions to ensure compliance and occupant safety.
The rise of large-scale warehousing, e-commerce fulfilment centres and cold storage facilities is anticipated to create substantial 
demand for specialised suppression systems designed for dense storage configurations and sensitive inventory. The growth of 
the renewable energy sector, including solar farms, battery storage facilities and wind farms, could also create new application 
areas for tailored suppression solutions to protect complex and high-value equipment. Urban densification in developed and 
emerging markets is expected to fuel demand for compact, high-performance fire suppression systems suitable for confined

Overview of the Indian fire suppression equipment market
Clocked a CAGR of 13% between fiscals 2020 and 2026
Fire suppression systems are engineered solutions designed to control and extinguish fires automatically or manually. They 
include components such as fire suppression agents (including water, foam, gas or chemicals), and delivery mechanisms such 
as fire sprinkler systems and fire hydrant systems. The increasing fire safety measures taken across sectors such as 
manufacturing, oil and gas, logistics, data centres and commercial real estate in India has increased the adoption of specialised 
fire suppression solutions that can protect lives and infrastructure. For instance, clean-agent gas suppression systems are 
favoured in data centres to protect sensitive electronic equipment, while foam equipment & suppression systems and water￾mist systems are common in oil depots and chemical factories. In residential buildings, dry powder and sprinkler systems are 
being promoted due to their cost-effectiveness and reliability. The need for customised solutions is expanding the market 
footprint of suppression systems in India.

billion to Rs 82 billion. It is expected to see a CAGR of 11-13% during fiscals 2026-31, valuing the market at Rs 135-155 
billion.

Pricing of key fire suppression equipment
Pricing for fire protection equipment is dependent on several factors like type and quality of the equipment, raw material prices, 
manufacturer’s brand, configuration of the product and associated certifications. The type and quality of fire protection 
equipment, such as fire extinguishers, fire alarms, and sprinkler systems, hydrant systems, foam equipment & suppression 
systems, and gas-based systems can significantly impact the price. Complex equipment with advanced features and 
certifications (e.g., ISO, CE, UL Solutions, FM Approvals) tends to be more expensive. Also, credibility, and market presence 
of the manufacturer or brand can influence the price of fire protection equipment. Variation in raw materials like brass, steel, 
aluminium, copper may also impact pricing of the fire protection equipment.
In India, fire protection equipment are sold under diverse brands and with varied specifications and standards. The price of the 
equipment may also vary depending on the type of fire protection system being used, competitive positioning, customer 
segments and regional dynamics.

Key entry barriers in the fire suppression industry
The fire suppression equipment industry is characterised by moderate to high entry barriers, particularly in industrial and 
commercial applications. Some of the entry barriers are mentioned in the following table.
Entry barriers Description
Regulatory compliances requiring 
long certification/qualification 
cycles
A prominent entry barrier is stringent regulatory compliances, which require 
manufacturers to adhere to multiple codes and standards, including the NBC codes, BIS 
certifications, OISD (for oil and gas industry), environmental laws, relevant state and 
project laws governing fire safety.
For specialised applications, such as in the oil and gas sector or data centres, global 
certifications such as UL Solutions, FM Approvals are often mandatory, significantly 
raising the threshold for entry.
Furthermore, product certification process is time-consuming, often requiring 6-24 
months for new product lines due to extensive testing, documentation, approval from 
195
Entry barriers Description
certification bodies and third-party inspections. This significantly delays time-to￾market for new entrants.
Overall, fire protection is usually a highly regulated industry with long certification 
cycles, high compliance thresholds, and high-performance benchmarks. Additionally, 
several end-use sectors require specialised product approvals, industry-specific 
certifications, regular audits, and compliance with geographical certifications, which 
acts as an entry barrier for new players. 
High capital intensity High capital intensity of fire suppression equipment business poses a significant 
challenge to enter this industry. Setting up approved and certified manufacturing 
facilities require significant manpower and financial investments, particularly while 
seeking global certifications or serving large-scale infrastructural, industrial or public 
projects.
Big mandates also demand robust quality management systems, traceability, audit 
readiness, well-established supply chain, pan-India service network and good after￾sales service, each of which requires sustained investment and operational maturity. 
This creates significant challenges for new players.
Technical capabilities Product complexity is a major barrier. Manufacturing of fire suppression systems 
requires deep expertise in system design, hydraulic calculations and integration with 
broader building management systems. Hence, players need to invest dedicated 
resources for the R&D and engineering capabilities to meet evolving client 
requirements in these sectors.
B2B sales relationships Sourcing and procurement discussions in B2B segments like commercial buildings, 
industrial spaces, etc. are often influenced by long-standing vendor relationship and 
vendor empanelment. It becomes difficult for new entrants to win contracts as 
established players, who are already part of approved vendor list, may enjoy the status 
of preferred vendors.
To be on the approved list, new entrants would have to go through a lengthy and 
complex process that includes extensive documentations, checks, technical evaluation, 
compliance and audits. This can put off new players from commercial and industrial 
segments.

SWOT analysis of fire protection equipment industry 
S
(strengths)
• Growing economy: Economic growth supports infrastructure development and construction activities, which 
are expected to positively influence demand for fire suppression equipment
• Regulatory mandate: Mandatory compliance with multiple standards and codes, including the BIS, NBC and 
product- and state-specific laws, ensure consistent demand
• Government initiatives to boost manufacturing: Government initiatives such as PLI schemes, Make in India, 
etc., are expected to spur industry- and logistics-related construction activity. This will likely increase the 
demand for fire suppression equipment
• Diverse end-use segments: Fire safety equipment is used across various industries such as industrial and 
infrastructure (the infrastructure sector includes warehouse and cold storage, data centres, airports, telecom, 
ports, roads, power, urban infrastructure, railways, and irrigation; and the industrial sector includes oil and gas, 
petrochemicals, metal, automobiles, textiles, paper, fertilisers, and cement sectors), commercial (commercial 
and retail establishments (including hospitality), healthcare facilities, and educational institutions) and 
residential. This diversity in demand ensures a steady stream of customers and revenue
• Government-led initiatives: Government initiatives aimed at strengthening fire protection infrastructure and 
creating awareness are expected to positively influence the demand of fire suppression equipment
• High entry barrier: The fire safety equipment industry has a high barrier to entry due to the need for 
specialised knowledge, equipment and regulatory compliance. This makes it challenging for new competitors 
to enter the market
196
W
(weaknesses)
• Limited enforcement of fire protection laws: In some regions and segments, fire protection laws and 
regulations may not be strictly enforced, which can lead to a lack of awareness and adoption of fire safety 
equipment
• Limited awareness and voluntary adoption: Despite growing awareness, there is still a lack of understanding 
about fire protection and the importance of fire suppression equipment among many Indians, particularly in 
rural areas
• High competition: The Indian fire suppression equipment market is highly competitive, with multiple 
domestic and international branded players, which can negatively impact product pricing
• Dependence on imports: Dependence on imports for raw material and components, such as valves, nozzles, 
etc. makes the supply chain susceptible to global disruptions, including fluctuations in foreign currency, 
geopolitical tensions, policy changes, etc.
O
(opportunities)
• Increasing urbanisation: Rapid urbanisation offers significant opportunities for residential, commercial and 
other infrastructure projects, which can positively increase the demand of fire suppression equipment
• Technological advancements: Adoption of new technologies such as IoT and AI for better detection, 
monitoring and predictive analysis can improve the efficiency of fire suppression systems
• Increasing construction capex: Growing construction capex in end-use segments, industrial and 
infrastructure, commercial and residential, will likely create strong demand for sophisticated fire systems
• Data centre capacity addition: Data centre industry installed capacity is estimated to register a CAGR of ~32-
34% between FY26-30 to reach 4,800-5,200 MW by FY30. As these structures require specialized fire 
suppression infrastructure due to their high- value and high- risk nature, it will potentially drive the growth of 
fire protection equipment market.
• Positive policy and robust FDI support: Policy reforms aimed at improving the ease of doing business and 
allowing greater FDI in core sectors, including manufacturing, are expected to bring a positive impact on the 
establishment of new industrial facilities in India. As these manufacturing units are required to adhere to fire 
safety norms to minimise the risk of loss of life and property and, therefore, are expected to drive demand for 
fire suppression systems.
• Protecting critical assets amid regional uncertainty: Amid ongoing geopolitical developments, including 
tensions linked to the West Asia conflict, safeguarding high-value energy assets and storage infrastructure 
against fire-related risks will warrant increased attention. This is expected to positively influence demand for 
fire suppression equipment in regions directly affected by these developments, offering Indian manufacturers 
a potential opportunity to expand presence to these affected regions.
• Import substitution: With the increasing focus on local manufacturing and self-sufficiency, there is an 
opportunity to substitute imported fire safety equipment with indigenously manufactured products
T
(threats)
• Economic slowdown: Any downturn in the economy including major policy shifts such as trade sanctions, 
tariffs, etc., can significantly affect the construction sector, which can limit the demand for fire suppression 
systems
• Regulatory challenges: Any changes in existing regulations or mandatory requirements/ certifications for new 
fire suppression equipment can create compliance hindrances
• Raw material price volatility: Fluctuations in raw material prices, such as steel, aluminium, etc., can impact 
the cost of manufacturing fire suppression equipment and reduce profit margins

OUR BUSINESS
Unless otherwise stated, references in this section to “we”, “our” or “us” (including in the context of any financial information) 
are to our Company. To obtain a complete understanding of our Company and business, prospective investors should read this 
section along with “Risk Factors”, “Industry Overview”, “Other Financial Information” and “Management’s Discussion and 
Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations” on pages 21,144,323, and 327, respectively, as well as financial 
and other information contained in this Red Herring Prospectus as a whole. Additionally, please refer to “Definitions and 
Abbreviations” on page 1 for definitions of certain terms used in this section.
The industry information contained in this section is derived from the industry report titled “Assessment of the market for fire 
protection equipment in India, with focus on fire suppression” dated September, 2026 (the “CRISIL Report”) prepared and 
issued by CRISIL, pursuant to an engagement letter dated May 19, 2025. The CRISIL Report has been exclusively commissioned 
and paid for by us in connection with the Offer. The data included herein includes excerpts from the CRISIL Report and may 
have been re-ordered by us for the purposes of presentation. A copy of the CRISIL Report will be available on the website of 
our Company at https://www.hdfire.com/investor-relations/. Unless otherwise indicated, financial, operational, industry and 
other related information derived from the CRISIL Report and included herein with respect to any particular Fiscal/ Calendar 
Year refers to such information for the relevant Fiscal/ Calendar Year. For further information, see “Risk Factors – Industry 
information included in this Red Herring Prospectus has been derived from an industry report prepared by CRISIL exclusively 
commissioned and paid for by us for such purpose” on page 62. Also see, “Certain Conventions, Use of Financial Information 
and Market Data and Currency of Presentation –Industry and Market Data” on page 17.
In evaluating our business, we consider and use certain key performance indicators that are presented herein as supplemental 
measures to review and assess our operating performance. The presentation of these key performance indicators is not intended
to be considered in isolation or as a substitute for our financial statements, and other financial and operational information 
included in this Red Herring Prospectus. We present these key performance indicators because they are used by our 
management to evaluate our operating performance. These key performance indicators have limitations as analytical tools. 
Further, these key performance indicators, including the manner in which they are computed, may differ from similar 
information used by other companies, including peer companies, and hence their comparability may be limited. Therefore, 
these metrics should not be considered as an indicator of our operating performance, liquidity, profitability, or results of 
operations.
OVERVIEW
We are an Indian manufacturer and supplier of fire protection equipment and systems, offering a comprehensive portfolio 
spanning water, foam, and gas-based fire suppression systems, which are also generally known as fire fighting products. We 
develop majority of our products in-house with proprietary designs to meet national and international standards, serving high￾hazard industrial applications as well as residential and commercial sectors. According to the CRISIL Report on page 203, we 
were the second-largest manufacturer of fire protection equipment and systems in India in terms of operating income (revenue 
from operations) in Fiscal 2025 and the largest exporter by value (equipment) in Fiscal 2025. We have export sales in 49 
countries as of the three months period ended June 30, 2026 and more than 90 countries as of Fiscal 2026. With more than three 
decades of experience, we have established ourselves as a globally recognized and reliable brand.
In the early 1990s, critical fire protection equipment and systems such as deluge valves, alarm valves, and medium velocity 
water spray nozzles were generally imported, with lack of Indian manufacturers offering high-quality alternatives like UL 
Listed and FM Approved products (Source: CRISIL Report page 170). Our Company is the first Indian fire protection 
equipment and systems manufacturer to receive UL Listing for deluge valves (1996) (Source: CRISIL Report page 202). Since 
the commencement of our business, we have consistently focused on providing locally manufactured fire protection equipment 
and systems as import-substitutes. We are also the first Indian fire protection equipment and systems manufacturer to receive 
FM approval for range of products used in low expansion foam system namely foam concentrates, bladder tanks, proportioners, 
topside discharge devices and foam water sprinkler discharge devices (Source: CRISIL Report page 202). Further, we are also 
the first Indian company focused on fire protection equipment and systems manufacturing to receive ASME U (pressure vessels) 
stamp certification (Source: CRISIL Report page 202). With 21 and 87 UL Listed and FM Approved certifications, as per UL 
product certifications and FM product certifications respectively, we have the highest number of UL Listed and FM Approved 
product certifications amongst the fire protection equipment focused peers in India as of September 2026 (Source: CRISIL 
Report page 202).
Our business was originally carried on under the name M/s HD Fire Protect Co., which was established by Harish Dharamshi 
as a partnership firm on April 27, 1990. Our Company was incorporated on April 24, 1997, as ‘D.H. Fire Protect Private 
Limited’ and in the year 2005 the name of our Company was changed to ‘HD Fire Protect Private Limited’. Thereafter, on 
April 1, 2005, our Company acquired M/s HD Fire Protect Co., as a going concern along with all its assets and liabilities, and 
the business was consolidated under a single corporate entity.
As of June 30, 2026, our offerings are spread across 8 product categories, namely - (a) sprinklers, alarm valves and accessories, 
(b) deluge valves, deluge skids and pre-action systems, (c) foam equipment and suppression systems, (d) monitors and monitor 
211
nozzles, (e) systems valves and accessories, (f) water spray nozzles, (g) custom engineered systems, and (h) gas suppression 
systems, covering a wide spectrum of (a) industrial end use in sectors such as industrials, heavy engineering, aerospace, oil & 
gas, refining and petrochemicals, power & energy, pharmaceuticals, data centres, warehousing amongst others; and (b) 
residential and commercial end use in sectors such as hospitality, healthcare, retail, education, banking and warehousing. We 
are also empanelled with various customers across sectors where we have presence.
We operate two manufacturing facilities in Maharashtra, Jalgaon MIDC and Thane MIDC, spanning a combined area of 8.50 
acres. We have expanded the capacity of our Jalgaon facility, with one unit for manufacturing and another for a dedicated fire 
test laboratory, industrial warehouse and R&D centre, admeasuring 2.50 acres, and are also constructing a warehouse at Wagle 
Estate, Thane, admeasuring 0.50 acres, which is expected to be completed by November 2026. In addition to our in-house 
production, we also undertake contract manufacturing of off-the-shelf products as well as white labelling to cater to diverse 
customer requirements. In Fiscal 2026, we supplied our fire protection equipment and systems to 2,066 customers. We supplied 
our fire protection equipment and systems across 49 countries in the three-month period ended June 30, 2026, and across more 
than 90 countries between inception and March 31, 2026. This international reach is supported by a distributor-led supply chain 
for international markets and a stockist model for India.
We maintain a strong focus on quality, reflected in the absence of product recalls and a replacement rate of just 0.01% over the 
three months period ended June 30, 2026 and the past three fiscals. Our R&D initiatives are directed toward next-generation 
technologies that enhance performance, ensure environmental compliance, and meet global certification standards. We also 
specialize in custom-engineered fire protection skids tailored to client-specific requirements and are the only Indian 
manufacturer to offer certain advanced systems, such as a next-generation pre-action system. Our innovation pipeline includes 
a new deluge valve design, for which a patent application is currently under process. As on the date of this Red Herring 
Prospectus, we hold patents in the United States of America, India, Turkey and Saudi Arabia for "pressure operated fluid valve 
with configurable diaphragm arrangement", and two design registrations in India for "diaphragm of fire protection valve". We 
have also made a patent application in the United Arab Emirates in respect of the same.
We have supplied products at some of the key sites including master stream nozzle installations at India's space launch pad at 
Sriharikota, fire protection equipment (alarm valve, monitor, master stream nozzle) at India's largest refinery at Jamnagar, fire
protection equipment (drain valve, water flow detectors etc.) for the new Indian parliament building, fire protection systems
(deluge valves) at Saudi Aramco's Ras Tanura Sea Island site and fire protection equipment (deluge valves, sprinklers etc.) for 
Oman's Integrated Power & Water Plant Project (Source: CRISIL Report page 199). These projects highlight both the global 
acceptability and trust placed in our equipment and systems.
We are both India focused and export oriented, with a balanced revenue mix across domestic and international markets. The 
following table sets forth our revenue from operations from domestic and export markets for the periods indicated:

(1) Revenue from Operations is as per Restated Financial Information refers to income earned by an entity from its core business activities including Sale

(2) Domestic Revenue represents revenue stream specific to India.
(3) Export Revenue represents revenue stream specific to outside India. 
(4) Operating EBITDA is calculated as restated profit before tax plus finance costs, depreciation and amortization expense less other income.
(5) Operating EBITDA margin is calculated as Operating EBITDA divided by Revenue from Operations
(6) Profit After Tax (PAT) for the year is as per Restated Financial Information 
(7) PAT Margin is calculated as profit after tax (PAT) as a percentage of Total Income.
(8) Return on equity (RoE) is calculated as PAT divided by Average Tangible Net worth. Tangible Net worth is calculated as Total Equity subtracted by 
Intangible Assets
(9) Return on capital employed (RoCE) is calculated as earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) divided by the Average capital employed. EBIT is calculated 
as the restated profit after tax for the year/ period plus total tax expense plus finance costs and capital employed is calculated as the sum of Tangible 
Net worth and total borrowings
(10) Fixed Asset Turnover Ratio is calculated as Revenue from Operations divided by Average Property, plant and equipment, Capital work-in-progress and 
Right-to-use assets.
(11) Inventory days is calculated as average inventory divided by Cost of Sales, multiplied by 365. However, for the three months ended June 30, 2026, 
inventory days is calculated as inventories divided by Cost of Sales for the given period multiplied by 90 days. Cost of Sales is calculated as total 
expenses less Finance cost and Depreciation and amortization
(12) Trade Receivable days is calculated as average trade receivable divided by Revenue from Operations, multiplied by 365. However, for the three months 
ended June 30, 2026, trade receivable days is calculated as trade receivables divided by Revenue from Operations for the given period multiplied by 90 
days.
(13) Trade payable days is calculated as average trade payable divided by Cost of Goods Sold (COGS), multiplied by 365. However, for the three months 
ended June 30, 2026, trade payable days is calculated as trade payables divided by Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) for the given period multiplied by 90 
days. COGS is calculated as the sum of Cost of materials consumed, Purchase of stock-in-trade and change in inventories of finished goods, stock-in￾trade and work-in-progress.
(14) Cash conversion cycle is calculated as the sum of trade receivable days and inventory days, less trade payable days.
COMPETITIVE STRENGTHS
Well established global presence in a certification and stringent empanelment driven, high barrier industry
We have a business legacy of over 36 years, with our fire protection equipment and systems exported to more than 90 countries. 
We have developed technical expertise, robust manufacturing capabilities and a global presence in the fire protection equipment 
industry, which is characterised by substantial and enduring entry barriers. These entry barriers arise from a combination of 
factors, including the requirement for specialised and internationally recognised product certifications (such as UL Listed, FM 
Approved, ASME U Stamp, and CE Marking), each of which certifications typically according to the CRISIL Report, on page 
194, often require 6-24 months for new product lines. Added to this are stringent regulatory compliance requirements across 
jurisdictions, long product development and testing cycles, and complex, capital-intensive manufacturing processes. Sourcing 
and procurement processes in B2B such as commercial buildings, industrial spaces, etc. are often influenced by long-standing 
vendor relationship and vendor empanelment. It becomes difficult for new entrants to win contracts as established players, who 
are already part of approved vendor list, may enjoy the status of preferred vendors (Source: CRISIL Report page 195). Overall, 
fire protection is usually a highly regulated industry with long certification cycles, high compliance thresholds, and high￾performance benchmarks. Additionally, several end-use sectors require specialised product approvals, industry-specific 
certifications, regular audits, and compliance with geographical certifications, which act as an entry barrier of new players 
(Source: CRISIL Report page 195).
214
Among the fire protection equipment focused peers we are the only company to have all of the following certifications, UL 
Solutions, FM Approvals, CE, VdS, ASME-U and Lloyd’s Register, across the following product categories- sprinklers, alarm 
valves and accessories, deluge valves, deluge skids and pre-action systems, foam equipment and suppression systems, monitors 
and monitor nozzles, systems valves and accessories, water spray nozzles, gas suppression systems (Source: CRISIL Report 
page 202). These certifications are essential for participation in regulated and export markets and typically involve multiyear 
evaluation cycles comprising product testing, technical documentation, factory inspections and ongoing compliance audits. We 
are among the few fire protection equipment and systems companies in India to hold certificate from China National Quality 
Testing Center for Fire Fighting Products, (GUANGDONG) for fire protection equipment and system sales in China (Source: 
CRISIL Report page 202). With 21 and 87 UL Listed and FM Approved certifications, as per UL product certifications and FM 
product certifications respectively, HD Fire Protect has the highest number of UL Listed and FM Approved product 
certifications amongst the fire protection equipment focused peers in India as of September 2026 (Source: CRISIL Report page 
202). We also hold Bureau of Indian Standards (“BIS”) certification for stand post type water and foam monitor for fire 
protection, which is renewed from time to time.
Across domestic and international clients, empanelment typically takes 3-12 months depending on review complexity, audit 
scheduling, and documentation. Commonly assessed parameters include compliance with technical criteria, testing facilities, 
manufacturing and spare capacity, ability to manage concurrent commitments, adherence to safety, health & environment 
practices, and robust packaging and logistics standards. Our systematic and well-prepared approach has enabled us to 
consistently secure approvals and empanelment.
Our Company is empanelled with an international client through a rigorous multi-step qualification process, and, as per the 
CRISIL Report on page 199, our fire protection systems have been supplied at some of the key sites including Saudi Aramco’s 
Ras Tanura Sea Island project. This begins with portal registration, submission of statutory documents and certifications, 
followed by technical evaluations. Product catalogues are reviewed against client specifications, discussions are held with 
technical and sourcing teams across geographies, and a mandatory on-site audit is conducted to assess manufacturing 
capabilities, safety, environmental compliance, and alignment with client standards. The process is stringent, expensive, and
time-consuming, often extending over several months to years and requiring significant resource commitments. Upon approval, 
our Company is linked to material codes and recognized as a qualified supplier. Once empanelled, customers prefer sourcing 
from existing approved vendors for extended periods, making it difficult for new entrants to displace them. This creates a high 
entry barrier, further reinforcing the competitive advantage of qualified suppliers like us.
In select regions, fire department approvals are required, involving product certifications, third-party test reports, and regulatory 
clearances.
In India, empanelment with corporates in our end use sectors follow structured e-procurement pathways, requiring detailed 
company credentials, technical documentation, and evaluations of manufacturing and quality standards.

reducing valves, next-generation fluorine-free foam suppression systems, and high-performance foam pumps, each designed in

infrastructure clients for environmentally responsible, reliable, and efficient suppression technologies.

Leveraging in-house CAD modelling, simulation, prototype testing, and flow validation, we have been able to control costs,

A key milestone has been the introduction of fluorine-free foam systems, positioning us at the forefront of the industry’s shift 
away from PFAS-based products toward environment friendly sustainable alternative solutions. Supported by in-house R&D 
and performance validation capabilities, these solutions reflect our leadership in environmentally responsible fire suppression 
technologies. We are also advancing two major product lines: an advanced deluge valve integrated with pressure reducing

is a patented pressure-operated fluid valve with a configurable diaphragm, which addresses critical areas such as foam 
proportioning, valve mechanisms, and fluid control assemblies.

Deluge valves, deluge skids and pre-action systems
We offer a wide range of deluge valves in ductile iron, cast iron, cast steel, and nickel aluminium bronze (suitable for seawater), 
with deluge skids available in standard and customized configurations. Valves come with trims such as wet pilot, dry pilot, 
remote electric, manual release, and pressure reducing trim, ensuring reliable and rapid actuation.
Our Pre-Pack is a factory-assembled, cabinet-mounted pre-action system for water-sensitive areas. Using the dry pipe concept, 
water is only released when triggered, with double interlock versions requiring two fire detection signals for added protection. 
Electrically operated valves provide precise water flow control.
Systems are also skid-mounted and UL Listed for compliance and reliability. Configurable as single or double interlock, each 
unit includes an HD deluge/pre-action valve, riser check valve, pre-action trim, fail-safe valve, butterfly valve, pressure 
switches, solenoid valve, air compressor, nitrogen generators (if required), and a releasing panel.

Foam equipment and suppression systems
Our foam product range includes proportioners, discharge equipment, foam sprinklers, and a variety of fire fighting foam 
concentrates, with several models UL Listed and FM Approved. Foam proportioning systems include bladder tank 
proportioners, in-line inductors, foam ratio controllers, and balanced pressure proportioners, delivering precise foam-to-water 
mixing for diverse fire protection scenarios. Foam bladder tanks are available up to 20,000 litres capacity in carbon steel and 
stainless steel.
Foam discharge equipment is compatible with bladder tanks, pump proportioners, and in-line systems. Foam chambers protect 
flammable liquid storage tanks, foam makers safeguard dikes and tanks, and rim seal pourers are designed for floating roof 
tanks. Foam sprinklers serve overhead foam discharge needs in deluge systems, with many UL Listed and FM Approved 
models.
Our fire fighting foam concentrates portfolio includes AFFF, AR AFFF, FP, FFFP, and HD AR SFFF, providing effective 
solutions for a wide range of flammable liquid fire hazards.

Manufacturing process 
Our Company’s manufacturing process is broadly categorised into three streams depending on the nature of the product: 
standard products (with base of casting or forging material), fabricated products, and custom-engineered products. This 
classification reflects the different manufacturing processes used, while ensuring that every product passes through a structured, 
quality-controlled workflow designed for reliability, and compliance with applicable approval standards and/or technical 
specifications. 
Standard products include alarm valves, deluge valves, ratio controllers, foam balancing valves, bypass valves, water spray 
nozzles, foam-water sprinklers, standard monitors with cast bodies, monitor nozzles, and similar equipment. These products 
are based on castings or forgings as the primary input. Ferrous castings, which form a significant part of this category, are 
sourced from approved foundries, while non-ferrous castings such as bronze and nickel aluminium bronze are produced in￾house or sourced. All castings and forgings undergo incoming inspection before being released to production. The components 
are precision machines using CNC, conventional or special purpose machines, then assembled with other components and 
bought-out items. Each unit is subjected to hydrostatic and product performance testing in accordance with established quality 
assurance plans (“QAPs”), along with in-process checks at relevant stages. Completed assemblies are surface treated by 
painting, epoxy coating, or powder coating, followed by final inspection, documentation, packaging, and dispatch.
Fabricated products include foam bladder tanks, foam equipment, fabricated monitors, foam discharge devices, trailer mounted 
monitors, which are manufactured from steel plates, pipes, flanges, and profiles. The process involves cutting, rolling, forming, 
and welding, carried out by operators and qualified welders. Welding output is inspected visually and, where applicable, by 
dye-penetrant testing and radiography. The fabricated items are assembled with machined and standard components, followed 
by hydrostatic testing in accordance with the relevant QAPs. Protective coatings are applied to improve durability and corrosion 
resistance. Functional checks and final inspections are conducted before the products are packaged, documented, and 
dispatched.
Custom-engineered products are manufactured for project-specific requirements and typically involve specialised assemblies. 
The process begins with design and engineering, where fabrication and assembly drawings are prepared based on customer 
requirements. Raw materials are procured and inspected before being released for production. Fabrication, machining, and 
assembly are carried out under in-process quality control. The assembled products undergo hydrostatic and performance testing 
as per standardised QAPs, with client or third-party inspection where required. After successful clearance, products are finished 
surface, subjected to final inspection, documented, and packaged prior to dispatch.
Across all three streams, quality assurance is embedded at every stage of production. From incoming material checks through 
in-process inspection, hydrostatic tests, product performance evaluation, and final inspection, activities are governed by 
standardised QAPs and procedures to ensure compliance with contractual and other approval standards.
